source: Chen, Lin, Schaerli, Zhou (2023/2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Few-shot prompt makes the model run its code, read feedback, explain the code line by line, and fix it. Gains depend on how rich the feedback is. Unit-test execution plus explanation gave the best code-translation and Python results.
numbers: TransCoder C++ to Python, Codex: baseline 80.4, simple feedback 89.3, +unit tests 91.6-92.5 (text: up to 12 points). MBPP, Codex: baseline 61.4, simple 68.2, UT 69.4, UT+expl 69.8, UT+trace 70.8 [CORRECTED: Table 2c]. GPT-4 MBPP baseline 72.8, UT+expl 80.4-80.6. Spider (no tests): Codex 81.3 to 84.1 with explanation, +9 on extra-hard queries.
limits: Few-shot exemplars; 2023 models (Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, StarCoder). Table text was extracted from PDF layout, so cell-to-column mapping was checked against the prose.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for G2: revision from real execution output works. The gain comes from the executor, not from the model's opinion.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug (sample efficiency)
finding: Self-debugging beats resampling at equal sample count on Spider. One debug turn captures nearly all the gain; more turns add almost nothing.
numbers: Spider dev, Codex: debugging a greedy prediction matches the baseline with 16 samples; debugging from 8 samples beats the baseline with 32 samples. Accuracy change after the first debug turn is within 0.1 points.
quote: typically one debugging turn is sufficient, and the accuracy improvement after one turn is within 0.1%
limits: Spider only for this ablation; Spider has no unit tests so the stop signal is the model's own judgement. Appendix says similar on other sets but was not detailed.
agent_relevance: Supports a cap of one or two repair turns per attempt (G11, G12) and a rule: fresh attempt, not a fifth repair.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug (no execution ablation)
finding: Without real execution, self-debugging shrinks, and sometimes hurts. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were overconfident in their first answer. Execution-trace feedback (model traces its own code) was the most consistent self-generated feedback.
numbers: MBPP without unit tests: Codex 61.4 to 57.6 with simple feedback, 64.4 with explanation, 66.2 with trace. GPT-4 MBPP +3.6 points; other sets around +1. TransCoder Codex +3.5 points (80.4 to 83.9).
quote: both models tend to be overconfident in their own initial predictions
limits: Small gains within noise for GPT-4 on several sets. The authors' tie of the gain to GPT-4 internal knowledge is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Matches G2 and G3. If no check can run, do not run a repair loop. Self-traced execution is the best fallback, but weak.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug (error types fixed)
finding: Fixable errors are mostly near misses. The initial code is close to correct and the fix is small: missing WHERE conditions, wrong argument order, language differences made visible by running.
numbers: Spider fixes: wrong WHERE 25.7%, missing DISTINCT 17.1%, wrong JOIN 14.3%. TransCoder (GPT-3.5) fixes: 61.9% output mismatch, 38.1% runtime errors. MBPP (GPT-4): 69.2% output mismatch, 30.8% runtime errors; over 10% fixed by swapping argument order.
limits: Counts only successful fixes, so it says what repair can do, not what it cannot do.
agent_relevance: Repair is a local-patch operator. A wrong plan or wrong problem reading needs reframing (a different operator), not another patch.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: With the answer label as the stop signal (oracle), self-correction looks great. Remove the oracle and it makes accuracy worse. Earlier positive results leaked the label.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 after 2 rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels (Table 2): GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction.
limits: Reasoning tasks (math, commonsense, QA), not code. Table cells read from PDF layout. Generic feedback prompts; the authors say better prompts for a task could help.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1 and G2. Doubt on a schedule hurts. This is the control experiment our debug loop must pass: a signal from outside the model.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (why it hurts, and debate)
finding: The model keeps its answer most of the time, but when it changes, correct answers turn wrong more often than wrong turn right. Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at equal responses.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: 74.7% of the time the initial answer is kept. At 9 responses, self-consistency 88.2 versus debate about 83.0 on GSM8K (Table 7, cell alignment uncertain). Constrained generation: self-correct at 7 calls scored lower than a fair standard prompt baseline.
quote: The fundamental issue is that LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2 only; 2023 models. Reasoning models were not tested.
agent_relevance: Supports G4, G9 (no debate) and G5 (code selects). Also a warning: a critic prompt can pull a right answer off its place.

source: Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao, Solar-Lezama (2024, ICLR) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: At matched total sample budget, self-repair often does not beat plain resampling, especially at small budgets. Repair gains are modest, vary by problem subset, and are sometimes absent. More initial samples beat more repair attempts.
numbers: HumanEval and APPS (300 APPS tasks), CodeLlama-13b, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. GPT-4 APPS: 10 initial samples plus 1 repair each (20 total) = 1.05x pass@20; 2 initial plus 10 repairs each (22 total) = 0.97x pass@22. Fixing initial samples and raising repairs gave marginal or negative change at low budget.
quote: self-repair is bottlenecked by the model's ability to provide feedback on its own code
limits: Self-contained Python with executable tests; 2023 models. Unit tests are assumed available. Repair success and fresh-sample success rise together with easy tasks, so the sign is hard to predict.
agent_relevance: Strongest equal-compute test of a debug loop. Our schema (G7, G11, G12) should default to diverse fresh attempts and spend repair only on a located failure.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet? (feedback quality, human study)
finding: The weak step is the model's own explanation of why the code fails. A stronger model's feedback lifts a weaker model's repair above both baselines. Human feedback on GPT-4's failures raises repair success a lot.
numbers: 16 human participants wrote 2 feedbacks each for 40 failing GPT-4 programs, 25 GPT-4 repairs per feedback. Repair success overall 33.30% (GPT-4 feedback) vs 52.60% (human); introductory 42.64 vs 62.21; interview 19.33 vs 45.67; competition 3.67 vs 14.67. Boost with stronger-model feedback beat both i.i.d. and self-repair at all budgets for GPT-3.5 and CodeLlama.
limits: Small human sample (16 people, 40 programs); about one hour per participant; human-in-loop cost not counted.
agent_relevance: Fault diagnosis is the bottleneck, not the patch. A scaffold should spend effort on localisation evidence (traces, minimised failing input), not on asking the model to just try again.

source: Shinn, Cassano, Berman, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: After a failed run, the model writes a short lesson in words and stores it for the next try. On code, the loop uses model-written unit tests, so gains need no hidden test labels. A bad internal test suite makes the loop stop wrongly.
numbers: HumanEval Python pass@1: 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1. MBPP Python: 77.1 vs GPT-4 80.1 (worse). Leetcode Hard: 15.0 vs 7.5. False positive rate of own tests (all pass but solution wrong): MBPP 16.3% vs HumanEval 1.4%. Starchat-beta (small model): 0.26 baseline vs 0.26 Reflexion.
limits: Table cells were hard to align in the PDF text; MBPP row matches the paper's own text on inferior MBPP performance. Self-written tests. Authors' own report; no external replication opened.
agent_relevance: Memory of lessons works only if the stop check is good (G3, G6). A weak check yields confident wrong submissions. Small models gain nothing.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion (ablation on HumanEval Rust, 50 hardest)
finding: Remove test generation and the loop gets worse than the baseline, because the agent cannot tell when to stop and edits good code. Remove the written reflection and it does not beat the baseline. Both parts are needed.
numbers: GPT-4, Rust, 50 hardest HumanEval problems: base 0.60; no test generation 0.52; no self-reflection 0.60; full Reflexion 0.68.
quote: the agent is unable to determine if the current implementation is correct without unit tests
limits: 50 problems only. Rust compiler gives verbose error logs, which may help this setting more than others.
agent_relevance: Gives a measured rule: a repair loop with no trustworthy check lowers accuracy (G1, G2). The explanation step before the edit carries part of the gain.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: One model writes, critiques and rewrites in a loop with no outside signal. Gains are large on style-like tasks and tiny on code optimisation with strong models. Specific feedback beats generic feedback beats none.
numbers: Code optimisation (GPT-4): 74.8 to 75.0 and 92.9 to 93.1 on two metrics; GPT-3.5 14.8 to 23.0. Code readability GPT-3.5 37.4 to 51.3. Feedback ablation, code optimisation (ChatGPT): specific 27.5, generic 26.0, none 24.8. Sentiment reversal: 43.2, 31.2, 0.
limits: Metric is a model or heuristic score on tasks without a hard check; readability is judged partly by the model. Huang et al. show the effect fades under fair baselines on reasoning.
agent_relevance: Specific, located critique helps, vague critique barely does. Do not use this for correctness; a code run is the only critic with authority (G2, G5).

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024, ACL Findings) Debug like a Human: LDB, A Large Language Model Debugger via Verifying Runtime Execution Step by Step
finding: Give the model real intermediate variable values after each basic block of a failing run, and ask it to judge each block as right or wrong against the task. This beats Chen's self-debugging, which asks the model to explain or trace code in its head.
numbers: HumanEval, GPT-3.5 as debugger. Seed from GPT-3.5: baseline 73.8, Self-Debug (+Expl) 81.1, LDB 82.9. Seed from GPT-4: 87.2 to 88.4 (SD) vs 89.6 (LDB). Seed from Reflexion: 91.5 to 92.1 (SD) vs 95.1 (LDB). Gains up to 9.8 points across HumanEval, MBPP, TransCoder.
quote: LLMs are prone to mistakes when reflecting on program execution.
limits: Visible test cases needed. Authors' own runs of the baselines. Only up to 10 iterations compared.
agent_relevance: A concrete fault-localisation operator: code produces the trace, model only judges small pieces. Fits the rule that code gathers evidence and model fills a slot.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) LDB (iterations and granularity)
finding: Self-debugging by explanation plateaus after 2-3 rounds and behaves like repeated sampling. Runtime-trace debugging keeps improving up to 10 and more rounds. Block-level segments beat line-level and function-level on accuracy and token cost.
numbers: HumanEval, GPT-3.5, 10 iterations: LDB reaches 82.9; Self-Debug curves flatten near 79.9-81.1; repeated sampling flattens at a similar level. Function-level LDB needed about 8.1 iterations per program on average. Biggest gain on hard TransCoder items, +9.1 points.
limits: Compared at equal rounds, not strictly equal tokens (LDB prompts are longer). Difficulty labels were assigned by GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Repair-turn cap should depend on whether new evidence enters each turn. Without new evidence, stop after 2 (G1, G11).

source: Yang, Jimenez, Wettig, Lieret, Yao, Narasimhan, Press (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: With the same model, the tool interface alone changes results a lot. A custom interface with a linter on edits, a compact search and a windowed file viewer beats a plain shell.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, GPT-4 Turbo: Shell-only 11.0%, SWE-agent 18.0% (text also says +10.7 points over the shell baseline on the dev set). Full SWE-bench 12.47% (286/2294). RAG only: 1.31% full, 2.67% Lite. Edit without linting 15.0 vs 18.0 with. File viewer 100 lines 18.0, 30 lines 14.3, whole file 12.7.
limits: Truncated PDF read (text recovered through results and appendix). $1.59 per task on average. Ablations on a 300-instance dev subset, so standard error is about 2 points.
agent_relevance: Guards against bad edits (G2). A cheap code check on the edit (syntax, lint) cuts a known failure at no model cost.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent (behaviour and failure patterns)
finding: Typical run: reproduce the bug, localise by search, then loop edit and rerun the repro script. Agents rarely notice dead ends. Repeated edits of the same snippet after a syntax error are a prominent failure. Success is fast and failure is slow.
numbers: Solved by GPT-4: median cost $1.21 and 12 steps; unsolved: mean $2.52 and 21 steps. 93.0% of resolved instances were submitted before the cost cap. Average 14.71 turns on solved full-set trajectories, 75% done within 18 turns. Without lint guard 15.0% vs 18.0%.
quote: agents rarely deviate from this pattern but they rarely recognize dead ends or reset their problem solving approach
limits: One interface, GPT-4 Turbo and Claude 3 Opus; manual inspection claims, no rater agreement reported. Authors suspect (not tested) that more budget would not help.
agent_relevance: Evidence for G1 and G12: a long run is a warning sign. Add a progress detector that triggers a reset (different hypothesis) after N edits with no new evidence.

source: Jimenez, Yang, Wettig, Yao, Pei, Press, Narasimhan (2024, ICLR) SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
finding: Real-issue benchmark from 12 Python repos. In 2023, models solved almost nothing with retrieval-based prompting. Retrieval of the right files was a big bottleneck, and longer context lowered performance.
numbers: Best model Claude 2 with BM25 retrieval: 1.96% resolved. With oracle files: 4.8%. BM25 recall of oracle files at 13k/27k/50k tokens: 29.58 / 44.41 / 51.06 on average; in almost half of cases with the 27k limit BM25 found none of the oracle files.
limits: Original 2023 setting, no agent loop and no execution feedback. Numbers are obsolete for current models but show localisation as the first bottleneck.
agent_relevance: Baseline for the history: finding where the fault lives mattered more than writing the fix. Argues for a localisation state before repair.

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed three-step pipeline (localise file then function then line; sample many patches; filter with tests) matched or beat open agents at lower cost. The program, not the model, decides the order. Generated reproduction tests were the biggest single selection gain.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, GPT-4o: 96/300 = 32.00% at $0.70 per issue (highest among open systems then). Patch selection: majority voting 77 (25.67%) at $0.00; plus regression tests 81 (27.00%); plus reproduction tests 96 (32.00%) at $0.25. SWE-bench Verified: 194/500 = 38.80%. Authors found 4.3% of Lite tasks leak the exact patch, 10.0% lack key information, 5.0% give a misleading solution.
limits: Own ablations; closed-source systems scored higher (43.00% on Lite). Possible training-data leakage of Lite patches into GPT-4o, as the authors note.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G5 and G7: code-run pipeline with many attempts and test-based selection wins at low cost. A model-written reproduction test is a usable check if it first fails on the original code.

source: Zhang, Ruan, Fan, Roychoudhury (2024, ISSTA) AutoCodeRover: Autonomous Program Improvement
finding: The agent uses code-structure search tools (class, method, API calls) instead of file reading. Adding spectrum-based fault localisation (a classic debugging method that scores methods by which failing and passing tests run them) as hints raised the resolve rate.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: AutoCodeRover@1 19.00% (57) at $0.43; @3 26.00% (78) at $1.30; with SBFL 22.00% (66) at $0.47; SWE-agent 18.00% at $2.51. Full SWE-bench 12.42% vs SWE-agent 12.47%. Failure taxonomy on Lite: 29.3% right locations but wrong patch; 20.0% right file wrong methods; 18.0% wrong file; 6.7% no patch.
limits: SBFL needs a usable test suite; the SBFL run uses the SWE-bench tests, a favourable setting. pass@3 uses three runs and costs 3 times as much.
agent_relevance: An older debugging method (SBFL, E09 process models) works inside an LLM loop as a hint: the agent did not just take the top-ranked method, it used rank 3 and 5 matching the issue text.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Diversity Empowers Intelligence: Integrating Expertise of Software Engineering Agents (DEI)
finding: Different agents solve different issues. A model-based review committee that picks among their candidate patches beats the best single agent, but stays far below the union of what all agents solved. Selection is the weak step.
numbers: SWE-Bench Lite: best single open agent 27.3%; DEI committee 34.3% (+7 points, 25% relative); best group reached 55% resolve rate. Union (oracle) of 9 agents about 53%, while the committee picked about 35-36% (Table 2; column labels read from layout).
limits: The committee is an LLM judge, so G5 and G8 concerns apply. Candidates cost many agent runs, so not equal-compute against one agent run many times. The 55% group uses stronger closed agents.
agent_relevance: Shows the selection gap: the right patch often exists but the model judge does not find it. Code-based selection (tests) should be preferred.

source: Wang, Pradel, Liu (2025/2026, ICSE) Are Solved Issues in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly?
finding: Test-pass is not proof. Some patches pass the benchmark tests but fail the full developer test suite or differ in behaviour from the human fix. This is test overfitting in agent output.
numbers: Three tools (CodeStory, LearnByInteract, OpenHands) on SWE-bench Verified; 877 plausible patches. 7.8% of plausible patches fail the developer tests. PatchDiff finds 260/877 = 29.6% with different behaviour; of those 46.8% are similar-but-divergent implementations and 27.3% change more behaviour than the human patch. Manual check: 28.6% of divergent patches (22 of 77) certainly wrong. Resolution rates inflated by 6.4 points.
quote: causes 7.8% of all patches to count as "correct" while failing the developer-written test suite
limits: Three tools only; manual check on a sample of 77 patches; the differential tester uses an LLM to write tests, which could miss or invent differences.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G3: pass on given tests is not proof. Use held-out or mutated checks and compare behaviour with a reference.

source: Liu, Liu, Li, Tan, Zhu, Lian, Zhang (2025) An Empirical Study on Failures in Automated Issue Solving
finding: Hand analysis of 150 failed SWE-bench Verified cases gives a taxonomy of 3 phases, 9 categories and 25 subcategories. Pipeline tools fail mostly in localisation; agent tools fail in the iterate and validate stage, often stuck in loops on a failing approach.
numbers: Solve rates: OpenHands 53.0% (265/500), Agentless 50.8% (254/500), Tools Claude 49.0%. Causes of failure: about 65% flawed reasoning, 25% knowledge gap, 10% environment friction. Failed agent runs take on average 3.5 times more steps than successes. Iteration-stage share of failures rises from 27% (easy) to 64% (hard) for OpenHands. Successes: 80% within 19 rounds (Tools Claude) or 25 rounds (OpenHands); failures need 54 rounds to cover 80%.
limits: Manual labelling of 150 cases by the authors; one benchmark; 2025 tools. Proposed Expert-Executor fix is the authors' own and tested on previously failed issues only.
agent_relevance: Names the failure we must design against: persisting with a failed strategy (fixation). Supports a code-triggered reset when rounds pass about 25 without new evidence (G1, G12).

source: Liu et al. (2025) Failures in Automated Issue Solving (Expert-Executor)
finding: A supervising second agent that reviews the executor's strategy rescued some failures that the single agent could not solve.
numbers: Resolved 22.2% of the previously unsolved issues for a single state-of-the-art agent.
limits: Extra compute not matched against giving the single agent more attempts; tested only on hard cases the single agent failed, so selection effects and regression to the mean may be part of it. Conflicts with G9 unless the gain is shown at equal cost.
agent_relevance: A competing view on G9 and the fixation problem. Test only with a matched-compute control (same total calls, plain resample) before adding any supervisor.

source: Majgaonkar, Fei, Li, Sarro, Ye (2025) Understanding Code Agent Behaviour: An Empirical Study of Success and Failure Trajectories
finding: Failed trajectories are longer and vary more than successful ones. Most failing runs still find the right file. Fine-grained reasoning at function and line level, not file finding, decides success.
numbers: OpenHands, SWE-agent, Prometheus on SWE-Bench Lite and Verified. Failed trajectories longer: SWE-agent +12.6% (Lite) and +18.5% (Verified); OpenHands +31.0% and +82.5%; Prometheus +56.6% and +50.7%. Gold-file hit rate of failing runs 72-81% on Lite (about 60-67% on Verified); only about 27% of successful patches touch the gold function.
limits: Three agents with different base models, so cross-agent effects mix with model effects. Observational, no intervention.
agent_relevance: Failing is not mostly a file-level localisation problem. Check progress at function level and use length as a risk flag.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents (CodeAct)
finding: Letting the agent act by writing executable Python (instead of JSON tool calls) allows error messages to feed straight back for multi-turn self-debugging.
numbers: Across 17 LLMs, up to 20% higher success rate than text or JSON actions (as stated in the abstract).
limits: Truncated PDF; only the abstract and method text were read, not the full tables. Action format effects may depend on model training data.
agent_relevance: Execution errors as the revision input is a design choice already used in a deployed loop. Supports G2.

source: Pan, Saxon, Xu, Nathani, Wang, Wang (2024, TACL) Automatically Correcting Large Language Models: Surveying the landscape of diverse self-correction strategies
finding: Survey sorts correction into training-time, generation-time and post-hoc, and by feedback source (model itself, trained critic, external tools such as compilers and executors). It lists Self-Debug and similar methods as using a program executor.
numbers: No pooled effect size; qualitative table of methods.
limits: Survey ends before 2024; no equal-compute comparison. Read for structure and taxonomy only.
agent_relevance: Helps place our rule: only the external-tool feedback class is backed for correctness tasks.

source: Synthesis of Chen et al. (2023) and Huang et al. (2024)
finding: The two papers do not contradict each other. Chen's gains come with execution feedback or unit tests; Huang's losses come without any external signal. LDB and Olausson also say the model's own explanation is weak.
numbers: Chen: TransCoder up to +12 points with tests, +3.5 without (Codex). Huang: GSM8K GPT-4 95.5 to 89.0 after 2 intrinsic rounds.
limits: Different task types (code vs reasoning); our synthesis, not a source claim.
agent_relevance: Rule of thumb for the schema: repair gains scale with how much outside evidence enters the prompt.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) AutoCodeRover SBFL case study (django-13964)
finding: Without test-based hints, the agent was distracted by words in the issue text. With SBFL's top-5 methods, it found the real fix site. It did not blindly follow the ranking.
numbers: One illustrative instance plus the aggregate difference 19.00% to 22.00% (57 to 66 tasks of 300).
limits: One illustrative case plus one aggregate difference; no significance test; one run per setting.
agent_relevance: Execution evidence corrects a typical fixation on surface words in the report. Fits the failure mode 'superficial matching' in c21.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Failures in Automated Issue Solving (diminishing returns of interaction)
finding: Returns on extra interaction rounds drop sharply after about 25 rounds. Agents often enter a long tail of futile exploration. Cause is mostly reasoning rather than missing context.
numbers: OpenHands median 16 rounds for success; 54 rounds needed to cover 80% of failures. Easy-task failures still 41% (OpenHands) and 39% (Tools Claude) in localisation.
limits: Round distributions read from text; per-instance data not opened.
agent_relevance: A concrete budget: put a hard step cap near the point where success mass ends, and use the leftover for a fresh attempt (G12).

source: Search summary (2026) SWE-ABS: Adversarial Benchmark Strengthening Exposes Inflated Success Rates on Test-based Benchmark
finding: Reported by search snippet only: strengthening tests adversarially removed about a fifth of previously passing patches from top agents.
numbers: Snippet: rejects 19.71% of previously passing patches; top agent score on SWE-bench Verified drops from 78.80% to 62.20%. Not verified against the paper.
limits: Search summary only, preprint, not opened; treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: If confirmed, the test-overfit rate rises as models improve. Keep a held-out check in the schema.

source: Search summary (2026) agent behaviour study, repetitive loop pattern (arXiv 2604.02547)
finding: Reported by search snippet only: a GPT-4 SWE-agent run edited code many times, producing 28 syntax errors, without ever running the test suite.
numbers: Single anecdote from the snippet.
limits: Snippet only, not opened. Single example.
agent_relevance: Illustrates the loop failure that a lint guard and a mandatory run-before-edit rule would block.
